label: Relative Interior
notes: Open by asking what the interior of a line segment in the plane should mean. The ordinary answer is empty, but the geometric answer is the open segment. That tension motivates relative interior as the topology convex analysis actually uses when dimension drops.

label: Ordinary Interior Fails
notes: Use the three examples to break the habit of measuring every object in the ambient space. A square has ordinary interior, an edge does not, and a singleton looks impossible until its affine hull is remembered. The goal is to make nonempty relative interior feel normal.

label: Affine Hull Topology
notes: Define the affine hull as the smallest flat world containing the set, then define relative neighborhoods as ordinary balls sliced by that world. Students should see that no directions are missing by accident; directions outside the affine hull were never legal local directions.

label: Segment Extension Test
notes: Treat the extension test as a practical certificate. If z is in the relative interior, every chord ending at z can be pushed a bit further through z and remain in C. Conversely, if all those one-dimensional tests pass, z cannot be sitting on the relative boundary.

label: ri And Closure
notes: The closure laws are the backbone of the section. A convex set, its closure, and its relative interior share the same affine hull and closure; the boundary is the part left over. Theorem 6.1 is the geometric reason: moving from a relative-interior point toward a closure point stays inside until the endpoint.

label: Faces And Boundary
notes: Use the face example to warn against a tempting monotonicity rule. A face can be contained in a larger convex set while its own relative interior is disjoint from the larger set's relative interior. Boundary pieces have lower affine dimension and need their own topology.

label: Polytope Examples
notes: For polytopes, relative interior can be read from active inequalities. In the square, strict inequalities give the usual interior. On an edge, one equality is structural because it defines the affine hull, while the two endpoint inequalities must be slack. For a singleton, every allowed direction is already zero.

label: Products And Sums
notes: Present products and sums as calculus rules, not memorized identities. In a product, each coordinate has its own relative topology. For a Minkowski sum, choose interior representatives in each summand and add them. The closure statement is only an inclusion here, which is a useful caution.

label: Linear Images
notes: The linear image rule is especially important for projections. Relative interior commutes with a linear map because segment-extension certificates can be mapped forward. Closure need not commute as equality, so the slide separates the exact relative-interior rule from the weaker closure inclusion.

label: Intersections And Qualification
notes: State the qualification before the formula. If the input relative interiors overlap, finite intersections behave cleanly: the relative interior of the intersection is the intersection of relative interiors. The boundary-only contact panel shows why the condition is not decorative; without it the right side can be too small.

label: Numerical ri Certificate
notes: Turn the theory into a numerical inspection routine. First recover the affine hull from equalities or from the rank of point differences. Then test strict slack only for inequalities that are not forced by that affine hull. This is the computational version of measuring neighborhoods in the right flat world.

label: Degenerate Examples
notes: Degenerate examples are not exceptions to hide. They are the reason relative interior exists. A singleton, a ray, and a face all have empty ordinary interior in a larger ambient space, but each has a meaningful relative interior once the affine hull has been selected.

label: Rule Ledger
notes: Use the ledger as a proof checklist. Ask which affine hull is being used, which theorem carries relative interiors through the operation, and what qualification is required. The most common mistakes are applying ordinary interior too soon or forgetting the common-relative-interior condition for intersections.

label: Recap
notes: Close by returning to the lecture goal. Relative interior tells us to analyze a convex set inside its own affine hull. The segment test gives a local certificate, closure laws stabilize boundary arguments, and operation rules let this topology survive the algebra used later in convex analysis.
